title: Meta Ran Ads That Contained AI-Generated Child Sexual Abuse Imagery
excerpt: I've noticed on YouTube I see a lot of adult sexual ads. Things like home cleaning ads that have an unmistakable wood-grain image of fellatio. I've always wondered "how are these getting past the moderators?". I guess the answer is the obvious one: no one is moderating anything.
content_html:
I've noticed on YouTube I see a lot of adult sexual ads. Things like home cleaning ads that have an unmistakable wood-grain image of fellatio. I've always wondered "how are these getting past the moderators?". I guess the answer is the obvious one: no one is moderating anything.

Listen, we need you to verify your identity in order for us to not serve these ads to your kids. It's very important that you do this.

To quibble/add-nuance: The words have diverged into a false-friend [0] situation. It looks like the same word, but the correct/standard meaning depends on which language is being used at the time.

If someone is writing English and puts "billion" for 10^12, that's a translation error, much like writing "my grandfather became pregnant when he realized he'd locked the keys inside the car." (Instead of "embarrassed.")

Conversely, if I wrote a French or German sentence and put "billion" for 10^9, then I'd be the one making the translation mistake.

[0] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_friend

Which is a number that I should let sink in. Basically more than one piece of CSAM shows up in their ad stream every second of every day all year. If their moderation techniques are 99% effective that results in 360,000 CSAM ads leaking to the public annually.

Another interesting thought is how much would it cost to actually get that rate to 100%? let's assume human moderators aren't paid much but are infallible. That all-in a single moderator employee costs $65K , that's salary, benefits, HR ratio, psychological therapy, equipment, the works, all factored in.

let's say on average you get about 1 ad review ~every 2 minutes, so bout 250 ads per-day per-employee factoring in some time off you actually get about 65,000 reviews a year. So bout $1 per review. So the question begs how many distinct ads enter their system each year? which I haven't found a stat for. But assuming only 1 in 1000 ads are CSAM, which still feels high but is probably a reasonable ratio. we get 36 billion ads needing review annually. At a dollar each 23% of their gross annual ad revenue each year would be just moderation overhead and they would need to hire over 550,000 moderators.

Evil or not I think they organically built a thing that operates at an unimaginable scale, that even moderation with failures in the parts-per-million would result in tens of thousands of unsavory or unscrupulous ads reaching users and they have neither the incentive nor the capacity to reach even that level of accuracy.

With illegal behavior, we hope that we can make the punishment high enough that Facebook refuses any conceivable risk premium the perpetrators of that behavior would be willing to pay. [0] Do not tell me about CDA 230, I was there when the old magic was written.

blocks.html_en: Section 230 should have never applied to ads. Ads are a commercial relationship. Facebook and YouTube gets paid by these scammers so why would they want to accurately police them? The incentives are broken. Newspapers had to invent all sorts of ways to make sure that they had clear markers between ads, editorial content, and sponsored editorial content. Such things were enforced by lawsuits and a couple of Ad Bureaus. All of those rules should have applied to Meta (Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram) and Google (YouTube). Just as it was a sign that you were reading a bad/unreliable tabloid when you couldn't tell what was an ad and what was an article, Meta and Google should have that reputation already as vendors accepting payments for bad ads and whitewashing them as other sorts of content and it is still sometimes surprising to me that they don't.

blocks.html_en:
How is me installing that going to help prevent Facebook hosting unlawful adverts?

I barely visit the FB feed these days, about half of those visits being a notification that turns out to be someone's birthday.

Unlike FB themselves for the content they host, I find it easy to avoid them without needing the help of a filter, because on the rare occasion when I find myself being sucked into scrolling down the feed, this almost always stops within 3 items because that's how quickly I find the first utterly irrelevant item owing to how Facebook keeps trying to suggest (and advertise) nonsense.

The filter I want to see in the world is the legislative kind, the "Meta delenda est" style. This is of course *not* what Facebook would want: spammers want to break FB's filters, and FB would try to get past legislative filters. I count FB as a spammer trying to put ads into every third message you try to exchange with your friends.

sentences.zh: 我如何安装它才能帮助防止 Facebook 托管非法广告？这些天我几乎不访问 FB feed，大约一半的访问是某人生日的通知。与 FB 本身托管的内容不同，我发现无需过滤器的帮助就可以轻松避免它们，因为在极少数情况下，当我发现自己陷入向下滚动 feed 的情况时，这几乎总是停止在 3 个项目内，因为这就是我找到第一个完全不相关的项目的速度由于 Facebook 不断试图提出（和宣传）无意义的内容。我希望在世界上看到的过滤器是立法类型，即“Meta delenda est”风格。

sentences.en: This is of course *not* what Facebook would want: spammers want to break FB's filters, and FB would try to get past legislative filters.
sentences.zh: 这当然不是 Facebook 想要的：垃圾邮件发送者想要破坏 FB 的过滤器，而 FB 会试图绕过立法过滤器。

sentences.en: I count FB as a spammer trying to put ads into every third message you try to exchange with your friends.
sentences.zh: 我将 FB 视为垃圾邮件发送者，试图在您尝试与朋友交换的每三条消息中添加广告。

To quibble/add-nuance: The words have diverged into a false-friend [0] situation. It looks like the same word, but the correct/standard meaning depends on which language is being used at the time.

If someone is writing English and puts "billion" for 10^12, that's a translation error, much like writing "my grandfather became pregnant when he realized he'd locked the keys inside the car." (Instead of "embarrassed.")

Conversely, if I wrote a French or German sentence and put "billion" for 10^9, then I'd be the one making the translation mistake.

blocks.html_en:
I am not worried about that all nor any down votes.

Empathy for other people and the environment is a sign of intelligence. Those that don't think of how their actions affects those around them and the neighbors they will never meet nor the environment have an lack of intelligent.

Those that lack empathy are the same that idolize bad actors like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg. Greed and the desire for it is a high indicator of lack of intelligence.

There is a difference between being well off and greedy. I would argue that Steve Wozniak is a great example and better of the two Steves from Apple to highlight this.

I have created jobs and brought in international commerce to where I live. I produce solutions for companies I don't even know their names. I have kept people safe and will never know their names nor will their families know mine. None of which has deluded my empathy for others, human and non-human, and the environment.

My previous statement was codified in another thread. This statement is a two part. One to re-enforce my empathy and a social experiment.

I feel sorry for those that lack empathy. Empathy is the only way to put yourself in someone else's shoes. Intelligence is a by-product. There is no other way to live a life you can never have nor experience.

Label of _radical_ is something I welcome. When former co-workers and people you meet want to shake your hand before leaving after giving them constructive criticize, it is a surreal experience. Not when it first happens, when it repeats itself.

blocks.html_en:
I am not worried about that all nor any down votes.

Empathy for other people and the environment is a sign of intelligence. Those that don't think of how their actions affects those around them and the neighbors they will never meet nor the environment have an lack of intelligent.

Those that lack empathy are the same that idolize bad actors like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg. Greed and the desire for it is a high indicator of lack of intelligence.

There is a difference between being well off and greedy. I would argue that Steve Wozniak is a great example and better of the two Steves from Apple to highlight this.

I have created jobs and brought in international commerce to where I live. I produce solutions for companies I don't even know their names. I have kept people safe and will never know their names nor will their families know mine. None of which has deluded my empathy for others, human and non-human, and the environment.

My previous statement was codified in another thread. This statement is a two part. One to re-enforce my empathy and a social experiment.

I feel sorry for those that lack empathy. Empathy is the only way to put yourself in someone else's shoes. Intelligence is a by-product. There is no other way to live a life you can never have nor experience.

Label of _radical_ is something I welcome. When former co-workers and people you meet want to shake your hand before leaving after giving them constructive criticize, it is a surreal experience. Not when it first happens, when it repeats itself.

blocks.html_en: Ah, what a pleasure to imagine that scenario, however unlikely, for just a few seconds. People profiting from running unethical ads and child sexual abuse material, for whom financial gain is more important than any ethics, laws or health of others, who frankly speaking don't give a fuck about anyone else but themselves amassing more money, being held responsible and being moved to a new, very different kind of home behind bars. It would be as if angels started to sing and cleanse planet Earth just a tiny little bit. We would have reason to rejoice and celebrate. On the streets! On the roofs! Everywhere! Celebrate that the law still has teeth, and is upheld. It would also be a nice measure to heal other businesses from many bad practices.

blocks.html_en:
The problem is equating profitability with what societies want and don’t want.

Morality exists outside of the business world (and it should inside as well).

Further, it is a societies’ right to enforce the boundaries of what business are allow to do / not do.

For example: banning ads along roads and scenic areas.

Idk, the whole idea of “how much fines will I get doing X shitty business practice” is just gross. I’d rather see harsher enforcement to keep businesses on the straight and narrow more often than not.

sentences.zh: 问题在于将盈利能力与社会想要和不想要的东西等同起来。道德存在于商业世界之外（也应该存在于商业世界内部）。此外，社会有权强制执行商业允许做/不做的界限。例如：禁止在道路和风景区沿线投放广告。我不知道，“我会因为做X低劣的商业行为而被罚款多少”的整个想法太恶心了。

sentences.en: I’d rather see harsher enforcement to keep businesses on the straight and narrow more often than not.
sentences.zh: 我宁愿看到更严厉的执法，以让企业更正常地走上正轨。

blocks.html_en:
Perhaps, but when you're operating at any significant scale accidents become a statistical certainty. 0 screw ups, ever is not a realistically achievable goal. And if some limited number of screw ups is allowable, that necessarily becomes an insurable cost that amounts to "just the cost of doing business", so I don't really see the complaint.

Concrete example: If you run a construction business, even if you take all the required precautions, statistically you're going to get 9.2 of your employees killed for every 100,000 man-hours they work.[1] Is that proof all construction companies are evil, and we should shut them down for murdering their employees? Is it a problem that having to buy life insurance is "just a cost of doing business" for these companies?

[1]: https://www.bls.gov/charts/census-of-fatal-occupational-inju...

sentences.zh: 也许吧，但当你以任何大规模运营时，事故就成为统计上的必然。

sentences.en: 0 screw ups, ever is not a realistically achievable goal.
sentences.zh: 零失误从来都不是一个现实可实现的目标。

blocks.html_en:
First let's not use an unqualified label of "CSAM" when talking about generated images.

But if a thousand people see some ad then the amount of damage is not much compared to their overall business. I'd go for a healthy penalty on top, and adding in more transparency to make sure they don't hide the real extent of the problem, but it's still probably small to them.

Getting Facebook to put in a reasonable amount of blocking effort is good. But it wouldn't fully fix the problem.

sentences.zh: 首先，在谈论生成的图像时，我们不要使用不合格的“CSAM”标签。但是，如果一千人看到某个广告，那么与他们的整体业务相比，损失的金额并不大。

sentences.zh: 我会在上面寻求健康的惩罚，并增加更多的透明度，以确保他们不会隐藏问题的真实程度，但这对他们来说仍然可能很小。让 Facebook 投入合理数量的阻止努力是件好事。

sentences.en: But it wouldn't fully fix the problem.
sentences.zh: 但这并不能完全解决问题。

Out of curiosity, I've ran some experiments on Facebook for stuff like this.

Results:

- Reporting a message does nothing no matter how much the content breaks their terms of use. 100% of messages I reported bounced back in a matter of minutes with "no action"

- However, using the "request another review" function, which is available after the initial "no action" response, actually seems to work. How quickly this works seems to vary, I've had actions taken as result of this from 1 day to multiple weeks.

blocks.html_en:
Personally I find these kinds of things fascinating. Partially for the practical problem it represents and it's facets but also the one sided backlash of it all. Moderation is an interesting conglomerate of so many factors.

First of all I don't think Meta is a good or honest company, but that doesn't mean they're not trying at all. In reality even if they were good and honest I genuinely believe their task is probably nearly impossible. Humans just suck too much. It certainly doesn't help that Meta has at least some perverse incentive to be permissive with ads, as they get money from them. Though Meta execs aren't stupid. Inflammatory political ads are one thing, kiddie porn is another I suspect they lose more money over CSAM than all the ad revenue from them. I believe them when they say they removed over 36 million pieces of child sexual exploitation content last year.

Which is a number that I should let sink in. Basically more than one piece of CSAM shows up in their ad stream every second of every day all year. If their moderation techniques are 99% effective that results in 360,000 CSAM ads leaking to the public annually.

Another interesting thought is how much would it cost to actually get that rate to 100%? let's assume human moderators aren't paid much but are infallible. That all-in a single moderator employee costs $65K , that's salary, benefits, HR ratio, psychological therapy, equipment, the works, all factored in.

let's say on average you get about 1 ad review ~every 2 minutes, so bout 250 ads per-day per-employee factoring in some time off you actually get about 65,000 reviews a year. So bout $1 per review. So the question begs how many distinct ads enter their system each year? which I haven't found a stat for. But assuming only 1 in 1000 ads are CSAM, which still feels high but is probably a reasonable ratio. we get 36 billion ads needing review annually. At a dollar each 23% of their gross annual ad revenue each year would be just moderation overhead and they would need to hire over 550,000 moderators.

Evil or not I think they organically built a thing that operates at an unimaginable scale, that even moderation with failures in the parts-per-million would result in tens of thousands of unsavory or unscrupulous ads reaching users and they have neither the incentive nor the capacity to reach even that level of accuracy.

blocks.html_en:
Personally I find these kinds of things fascinating. Partially for the practical problem it represents and it's facets but also the one sided backlash of it all. Moderation is an interesting conglomerate of so many factors.

First of all I don't think Meta is a good or honest company, but that doesn't mean they're not trying at all. In reality even if they were good and honest I genuinely believe their task is probably nearly impossible. Humans just suck too much. It certainly doesn't help that Meta has at least some perverse incentive to be permissive with ads, as they get money from them. Though Meta execs aren't stupid. Inflammatory political ads are one thing, kiddie porn is another I suspect they lose more money over CSAM than all the ad revenue from them. I believe them when they say they removed over 36 million pieces of child sexual exploitation content last year.

Which is a number that I should let sink in. Basically more than one piece of CSAM shows up in their ad stream every second of every day all year. If their moderation techniques are 99% effective that results in 360,000 CSAM ads leaking to the public annually.

Another interesting thought is how much would it cost to actually get that rate to 100%? let's assume human moderators aren't paid much but are infallible. That all-in a single moderator employee costs $65K , that's salary, benefits, HR ratio, psychological therapy, equipment, the works, all factored in.

let's say on average you get about 1 ad review ~every 2 minutes, so bout 250 ads per-day per-employee factoring in some time off you actually get about 65,000 reviews a year. So bout $1 per review. So the question begs how many distinct ads enter their system each year? which I haven't found a stat for. But assuming only 1 in 1000 ads are CSAM, which still feels high but is probably a reasonable ratio. we get 36 billion ads needing review annually. At a dollar each 23% of their gross annual ad revenue each year would be just moderation overhead and they would need to hire over 550,000 moderators.

Evil or not I think they organically built a thing that operates at an unimaginable scale, that even moderation with failures in the parts-per-million would result in tens of thousands of unsavory or unscrupulous ads reaching users and they have neither the incentive nor the capacity to reach even that level of accuracy.

blocks.html_en:
Probably a case of "hate the game not the player"

CSAM is highly illegal, no doubt these accounts are getting banned but likely not charged (who knows what jurisdiction the advertiser is even in) clearly they're able to pass the current bar.

This is conjecture but I'd bet that in all likelihood someone at some meeting at Meta has floated the idea of moving impedance to the signup to try to limit this phenomena. Maybe more verification, or more hoops. And likely Meta crunched the numbers and was looking at billions of dollars lost in legit ad traffic and that just doesn't fly for a publicly traded company.

I'd guess that the folks at Meta would absolutely love CSAM to stop showing up, It's simply too dangerous, likely costs more than it earns, makes them look bad when it shows up, and alienates users who don't want to see it.

But those negative effects are probably all quantifiable to some dollar value that's less than the alternatives.

Executives don't get bonuses for altruism or ethical behavior. They get bonuses for making more money than they did last quarter. real fix is changing the game but that's a lot harder than it seems and can have many unintended consequences of it's own.

blocks.html_en:
Probably a case of "hate the game not the player"

CSAM is highly illegal, no doubt these accounts are getting banned but likely not charged (who knows what jurisdiction the advertiser is even in) clearly they're able to pass the current bar.

This is conjecture but I'd bet that in all likelihood someone at some meeting at Meta has floated the idea of moving impedance to the signup to try to limit this phenomena. Maybe more verification, or more hoops. And likely Meta crunched the numbers and was looking at billions of dollars lost in legit ad traffic and that just doesn't fly for a publicly traded company.

I'd guess that the folks at Meta would absolutely love CSAM to stop showing up, It's simply too dangerous, likely costs more than it earns, makes them look bad when it shows up, and alienates users who don't want to see it.

Which could be a "change to the game" but that might be worse. Protections like Section 230 are absolutely abused by large companies. But protections like that are also what has made the internet even possible

Overly strict rules can also be weaponized. Imagine running a site that supports user content, but any appearance of CSAM on your site was jail-worthy, and you get an email demanding bitcoin or you're about to get hit with some posts that will shut you down. You have good moderation but you know you can't withstand a literal attack, someone who can automate that attack and has a financial motive to get illegal content onto your site. what do you do?

blocks.html_en:
> 36 billion ads needing review annually

This would mean every single user gets 10 uniquely personalized ads per year.

Even if that wasn't hilariously unreasonable by several orders of magnitude, if the moderation cost was was included in the cost of serving ads, this would all self regulate and only serious actors would participate. Treating it as a public bulletin board while still raking in a percentage of the impressions for sure is a nice business model, but not what's best for the rest of the society. Maybe ads just shouldn't be such a lucrative business.

blocks.html_en:
> 550,000 moderators

You can bring this number down by only reviewing new/low-reputation advertisers, increasing minimum spend, rate limiting, etc.

You can also pre-filter for "definitely not CSAM" and only review the more ambiguous stuff.

I think your numbers are low too, surely a moderator can review over one ad per minute on average. And it may be more effective to split-screen multiple ads (with redundancy).

But at the end of the day it's a numbers game, something is going to slip through.

blocks.html_en:
Somewhat related: open YouTube in an incognito window.

Search something rather innocuous like "news". Click the first thing then go back to the main page. You have to watch through the ad.

The amount of slop you will get suggested as soon as the algorithm warms up is nuts. The ad you are first served might also be slop. I mean AI generated video advertising overt bogus cures (a memorable one recently - "did you know the Bible has the answer to Alzheimer's?") over AI slop footage.

When I compare to my normal/auth'd Youtube experience, it feels like a totally different app. I have never really experienced such a cheap illustration of the "Youtube rabbit hole" effect. The degree to which AI authored advertising is participating in this is imo pretty concerning if you have, in particular, older parents or relatives.

sentences.en: Click the first thing then go back to the main page.
sentences.zh: 单击第一个内容，然后返回主页。

sentences.en: You have to watch through the ad.The amount of slop you will get suggested as soon as the algorithm warms up is nuts.
sentences.zh: 你必须看完广告。一旦算法预热，你就会得到建议的斜坡量是疯狂的。

sentences.en: The ad you are first served might also be slop.
sentences.zh: 您首先看到的广告也可能是不流畅的。

sentences.en: I mean AI generated video advertising overt bogus cures (a memorable one recently - "did you know the Bible has the answer to Alzheimer's?") over AI slop footage.When I compare to my normal/auth'd Youtube experience, it feels like a totally different app.
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，人工智能生成的视频广告明显是虚假的治疗方法（最近令人难忘的一个 - “你知道圣经有阿尔茨海默氏症的答案吗？”），而不是人工智能的废片。当我与我的正常/认证的 Youtube 体验进行比较时，感觉就像一个完全不同的应用程序。

sentences.en: I have never really experienced such a cheap illustration of the "Youtube rabbit hole" effect.
sentences.zh: 我从来没有真正经历过如此廉价的“Youtube 兔子洞”效应插图。

sentences.en: The degree to which AI authored advertising is participating in this is imo pretty concerning if you have, in particular, older parents or relatives.
sentences.zh: 在我看来，如果你有年长的父母或亲戚，人工智能创作的广告参与其中的程度是相当令人担忧的。

blocks.html_en:
> In many industries, if you can't do something safely, you simply can't do it at all.

Absolutely!

Related story... my wife works in a regulated industry and she was running facebook ads for one of their new products. Facebook had just introduced Ai generated ad-copy and the ad agency didn't know that option was turned on by default so they uploaded all of the ad-copy that was approved by legal and then facebook was running all of these alternative ads that were actually illegal because the copy it wrote were all claims they are not allowed to make in that industry. They only caught it because one of the ads was served to my wife and she immediately noticed it was copy that was not approved and something they could not claim.

I always assumed these shady ads were created by shady people, and I think a lot are, but I wonder how many companies are unintentionally running shady ads because facebook generated those ads.

blocks.html_en:
> The car industry doesn't prevent accidents

The car industry is constantly innovating trying to prevent accidents and make them less damaging to occupants

> the school industry doesn't prevent bullying

They try to, though. There's all sorts of initiatives to reduce and prevent bullying. Whether or not they are effective, they are still trying and have been working on this for decades

> the nightlife industry doesn't prevent rape or drug use

There are tons of efforts in clubs and bars to make people aware of this problem and reduce occurrences of rapes. Drug use maybe less so.

> the telecom industry doesn't prevent scams

Yeah, they absolutely are shitting the bed on this one, I'll give you that. But they should be doing better.

blocks.html_en:
> I'm wondering what people expect these companies to do? Human moderators? Sure, but Meta products have approximately half the worlds population using them. At this scale it's pretty mind bogglingly difficult to moderate down everything. The ads/posts served per second is an astronomical number.

It's Facebook's problem if Facebook can't do the things Facebook is required to do. "Oh no it is hard"? Tough. Either they find a way or find they're no longer allowed to do this business.

> This truly is a case where AI is the solution. There's no way to automate this at scale with humans. As AI gets better hopefully detection and moderation will catch up

AI *might* solve this, or Meta's AI may be trapped in an arms race with advertisers trying to get around it for whatever reason has driven them to do this in the first place; but fully automated mass-generation of personalised ads was never a mandatory part of their business plan, so it was a problem they never needed to have.

There was just an outbreak at Taco Bell - should we fine Yum! Brands out of existence. liquidate their assets and imprison the executives, like some people elsewhere in the discussion seem to be advocating for? blocks.html_en:
> Ad pipeline is malware at this point.

Always has been.

Occasionally my girlfriend will comment on something she saw in an ad, even buy things off them. Thing is though that ad platforms don't seem to be doing anything meaningful to stop bad actors.

So really, clicking any ad and interacting with it amounts to placing your trust in a total stranger with the only criteria being they paid a little bit of money for you to see them. To which you will then download their software, give them your credit card, or whatever the end goal is.

It's far easier to assume anything in an advertisement is a scam and block them accordingly.

> At this scale it's pretty mind bogglingly difficult to moderate down everything.

Well that means don't do the thing that you can't control, or they shouldn't be legally allowed to do the thing they can't control.

Fine them out of existence.

blocks.html_en:
tbf they generally don't even try with moderation. A few years back they made a multimillion pound settlement with a UK consumer finance guru who was sick his face being used to fake endorsements of scam products promoted mainly via Facebook ads

So you'd think that a sophisticated tech company that had paid that financial penalty would find it pretty easy to have a simple text filter for "Martin Lewis" and perhaps even an image filter for his very distinctive face which pushed those ads into a moderation queue, particularly if they both appear together in the scam-ridden investment opportunity category and the advertiser is a new one (that's probably not going to stick around under that name for very long). But no, they remained a common theme for years afterwards...

And, as the sibling ad points out, if you report stuff that's obvious scams you get told they've reviewed it and found it to be OK. Plus you get more of it promoted into your feed because hitting the report button is a form of interaction with it...

I actually had some sympathy for Facebook when they were condemned for not moderating fake news from Myanmar they have no real capacity to moderate, or condemned for daring to slap the gentlest of content warnings on antivax stuff in contexts they understand perfectly well... but when it comes to ads they get paid for, which is a much smaller fraction of Facebook content that is unambiguously not protected speech or a matter of opinion, their lack of effort is quite something to behold.

blocks.html_en:
> I'm wondering what people expect these companies to do? Human moderators? Sure, but Meta products have approximately half the worlds population using them

In this case, we are talking about ad images.

1000 moderators x 5 second per image to click deny or approve.

So 1000 moderators review 720000 ads/hour

Per 8 hour workday: 5,760,000 ads

Per full 24h day: 17,280,000 ads

So we will use 3k for 3 shifts.

51,840,000 new image ads moderated per day.

At ~$1,000 per moderator per month (most jobs are outsourced to Africa and Asia):

$3 million per month $36 million per year

I don't see any public numbers for how many new ads they add daily but meta reported removing 159 million scam ads during 2025, so equivalent to around 436,000 scam ad removals per day.

blocks.html_en:
It's not everyone else's fault that executives etc. decided to grow their userbase/business/profits at all costs, i.e. with no concerns for the harms they've been causing. It's similar to how adding more and more code, more and more features, more and more stuff into software increases technical debt. Apparently "growth at all costs" for a business equates to ethical/moral debt, quite obviously in this case. Which shouldn't be surprising to anyone who understands/recognises the mechanisms of greed.

For software, sometimes paying off that debt means getting rid of some of your features/code/stuff. i.e. there's another alternative to "let's AI the AI".

scale the business down. shrink the number of users. make less money.

They make 200 billion dollars a year, 60 billion of which is profit, so they could afford to hire a million more moderators at first world wages (50k/yr) and still be making 10 billion dollars a year in profit, and that's assuming nothing else changed, if they stopped spending money on VR, AI, and other horseshit, they'd have even more money for moderators.

blocks.html_en:
Think of it as an individual and instead of social property real property. If a person is stealing retail goods every day, no one asks "what should he do?" what he "should do" is face consequences until he is not a person who steals every day.

Just because the social property giant corporations steal is somewhat abstract doesn't change any of the fundamentals of right and wrong. I'm so tired of this ultra-capitalist "right to be massive" assumption which places the value of unhinged monopolistic growth over maintaining social commons. What these companies "should do" is face penalties until they can safely manage their scale, or scope their scale to a level they can maintain safely.

blocks.html_en:
What a terrible outlook. “It’s not possible to do this thing safely at Meta’s scale” is an apologist cop-out. First of all, yes it is, Meta makes tens of billions of dollars of pure profit every year. They were that profitable while blowing tens of billions on the Metaverse debacle! They are not resource-constrained in any meaningful sense.

Secondly, if I’m wrong and it’s not possible, then you stop providing the dangerous service! There’s no reason Meta has to exist in its current form. If it can’t meet basic standards of human dignity in its product offerings, then it should change or cease to exist.

blocks.html_en:
Beyond these obviously deplorable ads, my wife got sniped by an ecommerce lookalike ad on Google the other day: a near-identical match of the vendor she was looking for, with a paid for sponsored ad (that was clearly linked to some chinese firm upon further review). Site had prices that were just a bit too good to be true, and a slightly different TLD that _I_ would've caught, but she missed because the price was a bit too good to be true. Only caught it when Citi asked me if I was spending 9000EGD on some random website.

And my point here is, we're in this great revolution of AI empowered everything and... these companies can't be bothered to scan this volume of AI ad slop to make sure we're not being actively scammed? Or having porn or CSAM spread? I understand it's a "perverse incentive" in the truest sense: they make money by taking the scammers money, but I was scammed once by an insanely clever lookalike Facebook ad, and had trusted their verified checkmark (about a decade ago)... with AI, these things should be a thing of the past.

If any of us did that clearly we’d be in jail for several years and put on the sex offenders register but when Meta appear to be hugely responsible for increases in teen suicide or crimes like these we get nothing. If corporations want the rights of individuals they equally should shoulder our shared societal responsibilities as well. The truth is impunity is the rule, victims especially of CSA and CSAM, or revenge porn, or of Mark or Musk's companies generating naked images of their body have basically no power, and its an exception when someone who is an abuser AND has any amount of social standing is put away.

blocks.html_en:
> The eternal question of tech platforms - should we be responsible for what users post?

I would never say a platform has to be responsible for what a user posts, and to be clear, I mean either a user of the platform, or a user of the platform's ad tooling, or anything else. Anything that arrives via an upload button of some sort. However: If you as a platform then distribute what has been posted, yes, you are responsible for it. Your service is now broadcasting that content. If that content is harmful, you should be held responsible.

Who else conceivably could be? And if the response to this is "well we have way too much stuff coming in to moderate it" okay, then restrict how much stuff comes in. Require approval on individual posts or on accounts.

Like, this is such basic shit. If a newspaper printed CSAM on the front page, they would be arrested within the day. But because Facebook is real super big they just don't have to take care of their house? Ridiculous.

blocks.html_en:
Facebook absolutely could remain a going concern while dealing with all of these problems, the problem is that they would be spending money to lose money.

One of the more perverse aspects of risk prevention is that riskier customers are often way more lucrative. It's kind of inherent to the notion that markets price risk into transactions. The thing is, illegal behavior is also just a particular kind of risk: if someone wants to sell nudify apps or scam old people, Facebook could conceivably be on the hook[0] for damages if they're caught. And in a sense, a risk premium is just a fancy kind of bribe: if Facebook won't take my ads because they think they're too risky, then I'll just pay more and more until Facebook accepts them.

With illegal behavior, we hope that we can make the punishment high enough that Facebook refuses any conceivable risk premium the perpetrators of that behavior would be willing to pay. The problem is that Facebook is really desperate for any increasing growth story, and when you're too big to fail, your growth story is to drip-feed enshittify your stack. Increasing tolerance for illegal behavior is downstream of this: you cut enforcement, tell them to automate more, they become easier to bypass... and you make more money. Because it turns out all that risky behavior... is only risky for normal people. Facebook can launder[1] the risk away and make a tidy profit.

[0] Do not tell me about CDA 230, I was there when the old magic was written.

[1] See also, HSBC turning themselves into a literal money laundering operation.

blocks.html_en: With illegal behavior, we hope that we can make the punishment high enough that Facebook refuses any conceivable risk premium the perpetrators of that behavior would be willing to pay. The problem is that Facebook is really desperate for any increasing growth story, and when you're too big to fail, your growth story is to drip-feed enshittify your stack. Increasing tolerance for illegal behavior is downstream of this: you cut enforcement, tell them to automate more, they become easier to bypass... and you make more money. Because it turns out all that risky behavior... is only risky for normal people. Facebook can launder[1] the risk away and make a tidy profit.

blocks.html_en:
We used to say computers can't make decisions because they can't meaningfully be held responsible for those decisions. Now the vibe seems to be that computers should make decisions because instead of anyone being held responsible we can just say "the computer made a mistake and it is very sorry" and effectively shield anyone from being responsible. But the thing is, machines don't do stuff. Not from a responsibility standpoint. My car doesn't drive, I do. It may provide the means, but I decide where we're going and how we're going there. Even with the active cruise on, the car didn't speed, I did. The car may have hit the wall, but I caused the accident. the car ran that person over, but I killed someone, not the car. The machine did what someone told it to do. If someone told it to do a bad thing, or someone did a bad job telling it not to a bad thing, that person is responsible.

When people started using Grok to make CSAM the platform's response was to paywall image generation. If we don't start making the driver responsible for what the car does, the coder responsible for what the code does, the CEO responsible for what the company does, they will continue to exploit people in increasingly horiffic ways.

(This reminds me of, and not to be political. This is a technological, rather than political angle) There's a TED talk by Carole Cadwalladr about "Facebook's role in Brexit" in which she talks about the ads the Leave campaign ran. This is what is meant by Facebook's "breaking democracy", where campaigns don't have to go through the usual disclosure avenues

Are there reasons why Brexit might have been popular? Yes, in the sense I've heard about them. Should we then be blaming Facebook?

The problem is consolidated power. Carole herself said in her talk that it's not about Trump vs no Trump (sorry. It's been a bit since I've seen the talk. I shouldn't just paraphrase), it's about citizens' right to meaningfully choose in an information landscape

This is the problem with Facebook. It becomes an Everything App. Who cares about fraud (say, on marketplace, needless to say the site itself, the way it's screwed over businesses) on the platform when you can grow big? Let's say in this case, the actual case I'm commenting on - "Facebook didn't know". Well then that's the problem, isn't it? It's a company set up by someone of low moral reasoning (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=1692122) that doesn't set out to make a good product, something people will actually like. It's about dominating an industry and ads can be totally unvetted or scummy or scammy if it enables them to do this

content_html_zh: 我注意到在 YouTube 上我看到了很多成人色情广告。 像家庭清洁广告这样的广告，带有明显的口交木纹形象。 我一直想知道“这些内容是如何通过主持人的？”。 我想答案是显而易见的：没有人在调节任何事情。Google Play 商店向我的孩子展示了一个谋杀悬疑游戏的广告，广告中床上有一具血淋淋的尸体。 该游戏的评级为 18+，该帐户上有我女儿的正确个位数年龄。我举报了该广告，一周后它仍然存在。 我换成了苹果。听着，我们需要您验证您的身份，以便我们不会向您的孩子投放这些广告。 这样做非常重要。不幸的是，我也看到过 iPhone 上儿童游戏的 MA 广告。 可能没那么糟糕，但也不是很好。 看起来比两年前好多了。你是什​​么意思？ 如果用户是成年人，您可以在 Chromebook 上使用 Linux，但如果用户是儿童，Chromebook 会存在一些限制吗？前几天报告了一个明显的性广告，并得到了一个非常人工智能生成的回复，以“亲爱的用户名”开头，表示他们审查了该广告，没有发现任何问题。在我完全放弃 Facebook 之前，我举报了一个明显的口交广告，并收到了类似的回应，而那是在人工智能发展之前。 我真的不认为他们曾经关心过。当你在 Facebook 的网站上举报犯罪活动、猖獗且有据可查的诈骗行为时，Facebook 确实是在欺骗你。 他们回信告诉您这并不违反他们的政策，并询问您是否愿意为您的个人问题提供支持。绝对地。 我叔叔被一个据称得到沃伦·巴菲特认可的“投资俱乐部”接纳，并由一些真正的金融人士负责日常运作。所有的沟通都是通过 WhatsApp 进行的。 他们从真实的股票提示开始（实际上非​​常好！） 然后进行了拉高和转储。请参阅：https://www.cleuremissionfund.com/我收到了类似的广告（我的广告来自鲨鱼缸人），进行了举报并收到了与您所描述的类似的消息。 他们显然是在盗用马克·库班的肖像并兜售明显的骗局。第 230 条不应该适用于广告。 广告是一种商业关系。 Facebook 和 YouTube 收到了这些骗子的报酬，那么他们为什么要准确地监管他们呢？ 激励措施被打破。 报纸必须发明各种方法来确保广告、社论内容和赞助社论内容之间有清晰的标记。 这些事情是通过诉讼和几个广告局强制执行的。 所有这些规则都应该适用于 Meta（Facebook、WhatsApp、Instagram）和 Google（YouTube）。 正如当你无法区分什么是广告、什么是文章时，这表明你正在阅读不良/不可靠的小报一样，Meta 和 Google 应该已经享有这样的声誉，因为供应商接受不良广告的付款并将其粉饰为其他类型的内容，但有时令我惊讶的是，他们没有这样做。第 230 条并没有规定广告商不能入狱，也没有规定 Facebook 不必告诉警方广告商是谁。谁会因为在公共场所展示广告而入狱？ 如果我经营一家商店，并将 CSAM 贴在我的布告栏上（因为我是被付钱的），那我肯定会进监狱。这里缺乏问责制是令人震惊的。我的例子是一条评论，上面写着“遗憾的是，还有更多[硬字]没有死。 我们需要清理这个地方”，并被告知这并不违反社区标准。有，但仅限于使用大公司的知识产权。 如果您将 12 秒的主流唱片公司歌曲放入专辑的视频评论中，则该视频现在属于该主流唱片公司。YouTube 如何检测电影和歌曲的简短片段确实很有趣，但多年来仍然有许多完整的有声读物被非法上传。自动检测与一个特定事物的匹配比检测与与其他事物类似的完全新颖的事物的匹配要容易得多。基本上总是有某种类型的过滤器，尽管不一定是我们想要的。 过滤器代表的目标越大，打破它的努力就越多。事实上，还有 Android 上的 Revanced apk 定制，以及 Google TV 上的 SmartTube。我已经有 10 多年没有在我的设备上看到过 Youtube 的广告了（自从 Vanced 使 apk 定制变得流行以来）。对于桌面操作系统上的 YouTube，您还需要 Sponsorblock。 在移动操作系统上，您需要 Revanced/Morphe，因为它将 Sponsorblock 集成到应用程序中。我如何安装它才能帮助防止 Facebook 托管非法广告？这些天我几乎不访问 FB feed，大约一半的访问是某人生日的通知。与 FB 本身托管的内容不同，我发现无需过滤器的帮助就可以轻松避免它们，因为在极少数情况下，当我发现自己陷入向下滚动 feed 的情况时，这几乎总是停止在 3 个项目内，因为这就是我找到第一个完全不相关的项目的速度由于 Facebook 不断试图提出（和宣传）无意义的内容。我希望在世界上看到的过滤器是立法类型，即“Meta delenda est”风格。 这当然不是 Facebook 想要的：垃圾邮件发送者想要破坏 FB 的过滤器，而 FB 会试图绕过立法过滤器。 我将 FB 视为垃圾邮件发送者，试图在您尝试与朋友交换的每三条消息中添加广告。多年来，YouTube 广告都是无可否认的骗局，因此完全不受监管也就不足为奇了。我只是不明白他们的算法。 我曾经向我的学生展示 YT 视频，但由于这种垃圾，我完全停止了。使用 unhook 扩展、ublock origin 扩展和 firefox。 另外，请毫不犹豫地使用 ublock 的“块元素”功能。 从大型科技公司手中夺回一些控制权:)伙计，昨晚我在 YouTube 上看到了一个“服装品牌”，上面有一个非常年轻的女孩穿着…… 不多，而且它不太适合所有错误/暴露的地方……报告了添加但该死的YouTube，怪异的假医疗广告已经够糟糕的了。YouTube 上更令人惊讶的是广告中明显的版权侵权现象。 整个平台似乎以版权执法为导向，但广告似乎获得了通行证。但这不可能是真的！ 从文章中（我添加了一个可能不相关的事实）：“性剥削是可怕的，我们积极努力将其从我们的平台上剔除”，Meta（在过去两年中已经解雇并解散了所有负责此事的团队）发言人表示。最糟糕的广告是带有各种性暗示的阴暗游戏。 无论您举报多少次、屏蔽广告或选择“减少游戏广告”选项，它们都不会结束。Firefox 和 uBlock Origin 将阻止您看到任何广告。 我什至不想使用它，直到添加变得如此重复。这是千真万确的。 当你拥有十亿用户时，你实际上可能会失去数亿用户，但这不会造成任何影响。 唯一的办法就是让政府参与进来并对其进行监管，并继续对他们进行巨额罚款，这确实会削弱他们的底线。对于很多人来说，政府的这种监管是不可取的，但在什么时候有人需要放下锤子来阻止这种情况呢？我猜你已经习惯了十亿（一百万）的标准。
